In Next.js, routes are rendered on the server by default. This often means the client has to wait for a server response before a new route can be shown. Next.js comes with built-in [prefetching](#prefetching), [streaming](#streaming), and [client-side transitions](#client-side-transitions) ensuring navigation stays fast and responsive.

This guide explains how navigation works in Next.js and how you can optimize it for [dynamic routes](#dynamic-routes-without-loadingtsx) and [slow networks](#slow-networks).

## How navigation works

To understand how navigation works in Next.js, it helps to be familiar with the following concepts:

00188| ## Organizing your project

00192| ### Component hierarchy

00197| - `template.js`
00198| - `error.js` (React error boundary)
00199| - `loading.js` (React suspense boundary)

00221| ### Colocation
00222| 
00223| In the `app` directory, nested folders define route structure. Each folder represents a route segment that is mapped to a corresponding segment in a URL path.
00224| 
00225| However, even though route structure is defined through folders, a route is **not publicly accessible** until a `page.js` or `route.js` file is added to a route segment.
00226| 
00227| <Image
00228|   alt="A diagram showing how a route is not publicly accessible until a page.js or route.js file is added to a route segment."
00229|   srcLight="/docs/light/project-organization-not-routable.png"
00230|   srcDark="/docs/dark/project-organization-not-routable.png"
00231|   width="1600"
00232|   height="444"
00233| />

00235| And, even when a route is made publicly accessible, only the **content returned** by `page.js` or `route.js` is sent to the client.
00236| 
00237| <Image
00238|   alt="A diagram showing how page.js and route.js files make routes publicly accessible."
00239|   srcLight="/docs/light/project-organization-routable.png"
00240|   srcDark="/docs/dark/project-organization-routable.png"
00241|   width="1600"
00242|   height="687"
00243| />

00247| <Image
00248|   alt="A diagram showing colocated project files are not routable even when a segment contains a page.js or route.js file."
00249|   srcLight="/docs/light/project-organization-colocation.png"
00250|   srcDark="/docs/dark/project-organization-colocation.png"
00251|   width="1600"
00252|   height="1011"
00253| />

00256| 
00257| ### Private folders
00258| 
00259| Private folders can be created by prefixing a folder with an underscore: `_folderName`

00263| <Image
00264|   alt="An example folder structure using private folders"

00267|   width="1600"
00268|   height="849"

00271| Since files in the `app` directory can be [safely colocated by default](#colocation), private folders are not required for colocation. However, they can be useful for:

00281| > - You can create URL segments that start with an underscore by prefixing the folder name with `%5F` (the URL-encoded form of an underscore): `%5FfolderName`.

00294|   width="1600"

00296| />
00297| 
00298| Route groups are useful for:

00304|

00306| 
00307| Next.js supports storing application code (including `app`) inside an optional [`src` folder](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/src-folder). This separates application code from project configuration files which mostly live in the root of a project.

00317| ## Examples

00323| ### Store project files outside of `app`
00324| 
00325| This strategy stores all application code in shared folders in the **root of your project** and keeps the `app` directory purely for routing purposes.
00326| 
00327| <Image
00328|   alt="An example folder structure with project files outside of app"
00329|   srcLight="/docs/light/project-organization-project-root.png"
00330|   srcDark="/docs/dark/project-organization-project-root.png"
00331|   width="1600"
00332|   height="849"
00333| />
00334| 
00335| ### Store project files in top-level folders inside of `app`
00336| 
00337| This strategy stores all application code in shared folders in the **root of the `app` directory**.
00338| 
00339| <Image
00340|   alt="An example folder structure with project files inside app"
00341|   srcLight="/docs/light/project-organization-app-root.png"
00342|   srcDark="/docs/dark/project-organization-app-root.png"
00343|   width="1600"
00344|   height="849"
00345| />
00346| 
00347| ### Split project files by feature or route
00348| 
00349| This strategy stores globally shared application code in the root `app` directory and **splits** more specific application code into the route segments that use them.
00350| 
00351| <Image
00352|   alt="An example folder structure with project files split by feature or route"
00353|   srcLight="/docs/light/project-organization-app-root-split.png"
00354|   srcDark="/docs/dark/project-organization-app-root-split.png"
00355|   width="1600"
00356|   height="1011"
00357| />
00358| 
00359| ### Organize routes without affecting the URL path
00360| 
00361| To organize routes without affecting the URL, create a group to keep related routes together. The folders in parenthesis will be omitted from the URL (e.g. `(marketing)` or `(shop)`).
00362| 
00363| <Image
00364|   alt="Organizing Routes with Route Groups"
00365|   srcLight="/docs/light/route-group-organisation.png"
00366|   srcDark="/docs/dark/route-group-organisation.png"
00367|   width="1600"
00368|   height="930"
00369| />
00370| 
00371| Even though routes inside `(marketing)` and `(shop)` share the same URL hierarchy, you can create a different layout for each group by adding a `layout.js` file inside their folders. These layouts nest within the existing app layout.
00372| 
00373| <Image
00374|   alt="Route Groups with Multiple Layouts"
00375|   srcLight="/docs/light/route-group-multiple-layouts.png"
00376|   srcDark="/docs/dark/route-group-multiple-layouts.png"
00377|   width="1600"
00378|   height="768"
00379| />
00380| 
00381| ### Opting specific segments into a layout
00382| 
00383| To opt specific routes into a layout, create a new route group (e.g. `(shop)`) and move the routes that share the same layout into the group (e.g. `account` and `cart`). The routes outside of the group will not share the layout (e.g. `checkout`).
00384| 
00385| <Image
00386|   alt="Route Groups with Opt-in Layouts"
00387|   srcLight="/docs/light/route-group-opt-in-layouts.png"
00388|   srcDark="/docs/dark/route-group-opt-in-layouts.png"
00389|   width="1600"

00393| ### Opting for loading skeletons on a specific route
00394| 
00395| To apply a [loading skeleton](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading) via a `loading.js` file to a specific route, create a new route group (e.g., `/(overview)`) and then move your `loading.tsx` inside that route group.

This is useful for partitioning an application into sections that have a completely different UI or experience. The `<html>` and `<body>` tags need to be added to each root layout.
